name: AZD6234
lead: AZD6234 is an investigational long-acting selective amylin receptor agonist developed by AstraZeneca for obesity and type 2 diabetes, given by subcutaneous injection.[1][2] Its connection to appearance is body composition: it is designed to reduce appetite and body weight, which is why it is of interest to people following the next wave of weight-loss injectables after the GLP-1 drugs.

Amylin is a hormone co-secreted with insulin that acts centrally to promote satiety. The first amylin-based drug, pramlintide, found limited use as an add-on to insulin, and longer-acting analogues are now being developed for weight loss.[1][2][12] Efficacy results from AZD6234 trials have not been published; research is at the stage of early-phase studies, with phase 3 trials registered from 2026.[3][4][5]

paras: Amylin is a small peptide hormone that pancreatic beta cells release into the bloodstream with insulin after a meal; it is absent in people with type 1 diabetes.[12] It slows gastric emptying, promotes satiety through hypothalamic receptors distinct from those of GLP-1, and suppresses inappropriate glucagon secretion.[12] Pramlintide (Symlin), developed by Amylin Pharmaceuticals, now an AstraZeneca subsidiary, was approved by the FDA on 16 March 2005 for insulin-using people with type 1 or type 2 diabetes, and in trials was associated with reduced HbA1c and weight loss in insulin-treated adults with type 2 diabetes.[12]

A 2026 review calls long-acting amylin analogues a coming class of weight-loss therapy, and a second review summarises experimental data and early-phase trials of amylin analogues across the class.[1][2]

Reviews describe amylin receptors as heterodimers of the calcitonin receptor and receptor activity-modifying proteins, a structure that has guided the design of newer long-acting analogues. Amylin agonists act centrally to induce satiety and slow postprandial glucagon release. [1] A narrative review of amylin analogues for weight loss summarises experimental and early-phase clinical data across the class. [2]

The first-in-human trial, a single-ascending-dose study in healthy participants who are overweight or obese, began in September 2022 with 54 participants, followed by a repeat-dose safety and pharmacokinetic trial that began in November 2023 with 104 participants.[9][6] Further phase 1 work covers renal impairment (24 participants), hepatic impairment of AZD6234 and AZD9550 (28 participants) and relative bioavailability of subcutaneous formulations.[7][13][8][14]

A phase 2 trial combines AZD6234 with AZD9550, a GLP-1/glucagon agonist, for weight loss.[10] The phase 3 programme registered in 2026 spans obesity or overweight without type 2 diabetes (2,500 participants), obesity with type 2 diabetes (1,500), use as an adjunct to incretin-based therapies (500) and a further weight-management study (330) due to start in 2027.[3][4][5][11]

Phase 1 studies have examined single and repeat dosing in overweight or obese participants, renal impairment, hepatic impairment and relative bioavailability of subcutaneous formulations.[6][7][8][9][13][14] AZD6234 is also being tested in combination with AZD9550 in a phase 2 weight-loss trial.[10]

Phase 3 trials registered in 2026 cover obesity or overweight without type 2 diabetes (2,500 participants), obesity with type 2 diabetes (1,500), use as an adjunct to incretin-based therapies (500) and a further weight-management study (330).[3][4][5][11] No efficacy results have been reported.

The compound is a pipeline drug and is discussed mainly in the pharmaceutical and weight-loss-research literature rather than in appearance forums. It has no marketing authorisation anywhere, and access is through trials.[3][4][5]

timeline.event: Pramlintide, the first amylin analogue, approved by the FDA.[12]
Single-ascending-dose phase 1 trial of AZD6234 begins.[9]
Phase 2 combination with AZD9550 and renal impairment study registered.[10][7]

card.summary: AstraZeneca's weekly-style amylin agonist injection for obesity, with phase 3 registered but no published efficacy results.
card.note: Investigational; no published trial results found.

quick.overview:
AZD6234 is an experimental injectable amylin agonist from AstraZeneca being developed for obesity and type 2 diabetes.

Phase 3 trials were registered in 2026, but no efficacy results have been published.
quick.mechanism: It mimics amylin, a satiety hormone that acts on the brain and slows glucagon release after meals. It is also being tested together with AZD9550.
quick.risks: Safety is being assessed in phase 1 and 3 studies; no published adverse-event data were found. It is not approved.

chain: Acts on appetite-regulating pathways to promote satiety
Lower calorie intake and body weight
angle.text: AZD6234 is being developed as a weight-management drug, so any appearance effect would come through fat loss. It is not an approved medicine and is only available through clinical trials.
